slides.title: When Routers Count Forever
slides.body:
Solutions
Define Infinity as a Small Number
RIP uses 16. If cost = 16, destination is unreachable. Stops infinite counting. (Limits network to 15 hops.)
Route Poisoning
When a route fails, the router advertises it with cost = infinity instead of removing it silently. Actively tells all neighbours: "This destination is dead."

slides.title: Link State Routing
slides.body: Link State Routing

slides.title: Link State Routing
slides.body:
Definition
In Link State Routing, every router builds a complete map of the entire network topology. Each router then independently runs Dijkstra's algorithm on this map to compute the shortest path to every destination

slides.title: Link State Routing
slides.body:
How it Works - 5 Steps
Each router discovers its directly connected neighbours and the cost to each
Each router creates a Link State Advertisement (LSA) - a small packet listing its neighbours and link costs
1
2
Each router floods its LSA to all routers (not just neighbors). Flooding means forwarding it on all interfaces except the one it arrived on, so every router receives a copy
3

slides.title: Link State Routing
slides.body:
Every Router Knows the Full Map
Every router collects all LSAs and builds the same complete network graph — the Link State Database (LSDB).
Each router independently runs Dijkstra's algorithm on the LSDB and builds a complete routing table - no dependency on neighbours for path decisions
4
5

slides.title: Dijkstra's Shortest Path Algorithm
slides.body:
Finding the Shortest Path
Dijkstra’s algorithm finds the lowest-cost paths from one router to all others using a complete network graph. It requires non-negative link costs, as negative values can break correctness

slides.title: Dijkstra's Shortest Path Algorithm
slides.body:
Algorithm Steps
Set cost to source router = 0. Set cost to all others = ∞
Mark all nodes as unvisited
Pick the unvisited node with the smallest known cost - make it the current node

slides.title: Dijkstra's Shortest Path Algorithm
slides.body:
For each unvisited neighbour: if (cost to current + link cost) < known cost, update it
Mark current node as visited,  its shortest path is now final
Repeat from Step 3 until all nodes are visited
Algorithm Steps

slides.title: Dijkstra's Shortest Path Algorithm
slides.body:
Finding the Shortest Path
Two key properties
Greedy choice - always pick the cheapest unvisited node next
Relaxation - update a neighbour's cost only if a cheaper path is found through the current node

slides.title: Shortest Path Routing
slides.body:
Finding the Cheapest Path
In networking, shortest path does not always mean fewest hops 
It means the path with the lowest total cost, where cost depends on the metric used:
RIP - Cost = number of hops (1 per router hop, max 15)
OSPF - Cost = 100 Mbps / Link Bandwidth (higher bandwidth = lower cost)

slides.title: Shortest Path Routing
slides.body:
Network: A—B (cost 5), A—C (cost 2), C—B (cost 1), B—D (cost 4), C—D (cost 9)
Find the shortest path from A to D
Finding the Cheapest Path
Shortest path = A → C → B → D, Total cost = 7
Path A → D direct via C = 11. Path via C → B = 7. Dijkstra picks the cheaper one

slides.title: OSPF - Open Shortest Path First
slides.body:
Link State at Scale
OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) is the most widely used Link State routing protocol, used inside enterprise networks and by ISPs. OSPF solves both major limitations of RIP - the weak hop-count metric and the 15-hop scalability problem

slides.title: OSPF - Open Shortest Path First
slides.body:
Key Facts about OSPF
Algorithm & Metric
Uses Dijkstra; bandwidth-based cost (higher bandwidth = lower cost)
Transport
Runs over IP (Protocol 89), no TCP/UDP
Updates & Convergence
Triggered updates → fast convergence

slides.title: OSPF - Open Shortest Path First
slides.body:
Key Facts about OSPF
Neighbour Discovery
Hello packets to form adjacencies
Scalability
Uses Areas (Area 0 backbone) for large networks
Features
Supports CIDR, VLSM, authentication

slides.title: OSPF - Open Shortest Path First
slides.body:
Link State at Scale
RIP uses hop count - ignores bandwidth. OSPF uses bandwidth - smarter metric
RIP updates every 30 seconds - slow to react. OSPF triggers updates immediately
RIP limited to 15 hops. OSPF scales to any size with areas
OSPF has no count-to-infinity problem
